newsitem.title: GREECE: GREECE NEEDS TIGHTER ECON POLICY, REFORMS - IMF.
newsitem.headline: GREECE NEEDS TIGHTER ECON POLICY, REFORMS - IMF.

text.p: Greece's economy made significant progress in 1996 but macroeconomic policy has to get tighter and structural reforms be accelerated to attain the goals set out in its EU convergence plan, said the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

"Macroeconomic policy has to become tighter and structural reforms be accelerated to secure the attainment of 1997 goals set out in the convergence programme," said the IMF in its draft report on the Greek economy.
The IMF noted that inflation fell further in the first months of 1997 but pointed out that the downward trend in core inflation had been temporarily halted.

Greek CPI-based inflation eased to 5.9 percent year-on-year in April from 6.0 percent in March. Foreign bank estimates put April core inflation which does not include volatile food and energy prices at 7.5 percent year-on-year, unchanged from March.
The National Statistics Service does not release core inflation figures but the central bank and the nationa leconomy ministry are known to monitor it.
The report said it was likely that inflation would not drop below 5.0 percent in 1997. The government forecasts consumer price inflation to fall to 4.5 percent year-on-year at end-1997.

The IMF which called for the passing of legislation to make Bank of Greece independent, agreed with the central bank's approach in gradually reducing its intervention interbank rates in tandem with inflation.
But it stressed that a restrictive monetary policy alone could not bear the burden of reducing inflation without support from the fiscal policy, moderate wage increases and structural reforms.

"Provisional provisions of the IMF delegation show that the central government budget deficit will exceed the budget target by 0.5 percent of GDP, a development which might lead the general government budget deficit to a similar divergence" the report said.
A shortfall in budget revenues in the first months of 1997 was to be blamed for the projected divergence between the actual and targeted budget deficit, the IMF said.
Lower than projected interest payments on Greece's public debt could offset part of the revenue shortfall, it added.

Creative accounting could lead to a lower budget deficit but did not exert downward pressure on aggregate demand which coupled with rising unit labour costs eroded Greek competitiveness and widened the current account deficit, the report said.

Privatisations and the acceleration of structural reforms could provide much needed budget revenues, increase economic efficiency and improve the trade-off between economic growth and external balance, it said.
Greece's current account deficit widened to $4.5 billion at end-1996 from $2.8 billion at end-1995.
The 1997 central government budget deficit target is 6.2 percent of GDP against a revised 9.7 percent of GDP in 1996.
The general government budget deficit is projected at 4.2 percent of GDP in 1997 against a provisional 7.4 percnet of GDP in 1996.
The liberalisation and deregulation of financial services boosted competition in the Greek banking sector, it said.
The IMF also urged the government to encourage banks to adopt international standards for cost control and risk management.
The central bank should make sure that commercial banks and their subsidiary mutual fund management companies separate their activities, it said.
The central bank should be given the power to impose reserve requirements and set minimum capital adequacy requirements on money market funds, the IMF said.

Taxes on banking transactions that hurt the competitiveness of Greek banks should be reduced to international levels and be applied uniformly to all credit institutions and currencies in which assets are denominated, the report said. --Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
